title: BLOCKED! Emboldened State Regulators Just Scuttled a Major Money Merger
author: Lee Hepner
content:
When Hiram Johnson was elected the 23rd Governor of the State of California in
November 1910, the Southern Pacific Railroad was so powerful that most people
thought of it as the fourth branch of government. In his 1911 [inaugural
address](https://governors.library.ca.gov/addresses/23-hjohnson01.html),
Governor Johnson referred to Southern Pacific as "the political master of this
State."

Johnson was a Progressive Republican, one of many who had broken with
President Taft over high tariffs and conflicts over conservation, corporate
regulation, and the influence of monied interests. As he put it in his
[inaugural
address](https://governors.library.ca.gov/addresses/23-hjohnson01.html):

> In some form or other nearly every governmental problem that involves the
> health, the happiness, or the prosperity of the State has arisen, because
> some private interest has intervened or has sought for its own gain to
> exploit either the resources or the politics of the State. I take it,
> therefore, that the first duty that is mine to perform is to eliminate every
> private interest from the government, and to make the public service of the
> State responsive solely to the people.

Johnson saw it as his mission to replace every appointee who represented a
"political machine or a corporation" and bring in a new uncorrupted workforce,
so as to confront the "apostles of big business." He realized the result would
bring "a storm of indignation," but also, the liberty of a free people.

Governor Johnson's election was not a blowout; he won by just 5 points. But by
October, just 10 months into his governorship, he had persuaded the
legislature to deliver him a package of constitutional amendments,
establishing the statewide ballot process, the ability to recall public
officials, women's suffrage and, critical to this column, the strengthening of
the Railroad Commission. And the legislature delivered the constitutional
amendments by a vote of 35-1 in the Senate and 71-0 in the Assembly.
California's era of popular democracy had arrived.

Strengthening the Railroad Commission was a direct rebuke of the power and
influence of Southern Pacific Railroad and transitioned the entirety of the
Commission's appointment authority to the Governor. The other central reform
to the Commission was found in Section 51, the Commission's "change of
control" authority, which gave it new powers to approve any sale, lease,
mortgage, merger or consolidation of any utility property.

In many ways, we still live in the California that Governor Johnson reinvented
in 1911. The "change of control" authority first established in the Railroad
Commission is now integrated in several agencies, from financial regulators to
insurance oversight. In other ways, we don't. No one would argue that the
lofty ambition to rid government of every appointee with loyalties to private
interests has endured as anything but an ambition. And yet, in many places
across the country, including in [some](https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-
government/capitol-alert/article317927214.html)
[parts](https://thebusinessjournal.com/jane-kim-california-insurance-
commissioner/) of California, last week's midterm elections resembled a
populist wave, not unlike the rebuke of corporate power that carried Johnson
to Sacramento.

Then, on Wednesday of this week, an under-the-radar state agency, under the
leadership of former Consumer Financial Protection Bureau Director Rohit
Chopra, invoked its change of control authority to thwart a merger that had
until then escaped condemnation of political leaders across the country. And
it involved a corporation that was well known to late 19th- and early 20th
Century progressives, Western Union, which had faced allegations of
monopolizing the telegraph industry dating back to [at
least](https://www.jstor.org/stable/25101819?seq=1) 1889.

But it is very much a scandal of 2026, and wed to the political climate of
2026. One week after an election were economic populism rippled across the
country, a state agency was using the authority first established in the wake
of a populist revolt over a century ago to confront corporate power.

Governor and later Senator Hiram Johnson (L); CA Secretary Rohit Chopra (R)

The parallels to the 1910 populist election wave and Governor Johnson's
creation of administrative merger controls are too enticing. Could this be the
dawn of a new era in American politics? There are reasons to say yes, and
perhaps more reasons to be skeptical. But one thing is clear: public officials
at every level of government are waking up to new opportunities to serve the
public. With the right attention, those opportunities might well become
expectations -- as envisioned by Governor Johnson -- that government should be
singularly committed to representing the public's interest, free from the
influence of private interests.

### **The Western Union-Intermex Merger**

Last August 2025, Western Union announced an agreement to acquire
International Money Express (Intermex) for approximately $500 million. What
are these companies, and why did they want to merge? Western Union and
Intermex are two publicly-traded companies that provide money transfer
services, like the services provided by Venmo and CashApp. But whereas Venmo
and CashApp primarily service domestic money transfers, Western Union and
Intermex facilitate international money transfers.

Western Union is one of the world's largest money transfer companies, whose
customers - mostly individuals sending money to family, friends, and
businesses - can transfer money domestically, internationally and across
borders in more than 200 countries. Western Union makes money by charging a
transfer fee and earns revenue from the foreign exchange spread when
converting currencies.

[![A man sits on a chair outside a Western Union currency exchange office,
looking at his
phone.](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!0LIl!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F71bac83b-7880-4c04-86ca-46ff3d39894e_700x436.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!0LIl!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F71bac83b-7880-4c04-86ca-46ff3d39894e_700x436.jpeg)(David
W. Cerny/Reuters)

Intermex specializes in transfers from the United States to Latin America and
the Caribbean. Like Western Union, Intermex's customers send money across
borders, and Intermex makes money by charging transfer fees and from foreign
exchange spreads.

Another distinguishing characteristic of both Western Union and Intermex is
that they both operate through retail locations, which requires having
sprawling and robust partnerships with grocery stores, convenience stores,
neighborhood businesses, and other independent retail agents. These retail
partnerships are valuable in a merger transaction because, for services that
rely on physical locations, it's a pathway to automatic geographic scale
without having to compete for those relationships on your own. And Western
Union wanted Intermex's robust network of retail partnerships to expand its
own reach throughout Latin America.

Cross-border money transfers are also big business and are a vital resource to
immigrants, in particular, who can use the services to transfer money back to
their families. As former FTC Commissioner Alvaro Bedoya
[pointed](https://x.com/BedoyaUSA/status/1993394671884575205) out when this
deal was announced:

> Millions of people send money to help their family in Latin America. I've
> been sending money more or less monthly since I graduated law school almost
> 20 years ago. It's really important to have a range of companies competing
> for that business. When you're sending $35 or $50 to just get someone to
> their next paycheck (which is a pretty common thing), the fee for that can
> really eat at what you're sending.
>
> So I'm pretty shocked to learn that Western Union is buying a company that
> *already* holds >30% market shares in U.S. to Ecuador and U.S. to Nicaragua
> remittances, and a 29% share in remittances to Guatemala. Intermex also
> claims to hold a 20% share in remittances to Mexico, and public reporting
> suggests that Western Union is #1 -- in other words, *above* Intermex -- in
> that corridor.

These types of transfers reach into the billions of dollars per year. In 2025,
the New York Times reported that they had seen an
[uptick](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/09/08/world/americas/trump-migrants-
remittances.html) in international transfers attributable to heightened
concerns around deportation caused by expanded and increasingly aggressive ICE
enforcement. So the threat of retail locations closing down, or fees going up,
was a source of particular concern for immigrant populations and other
customers with family abroad. Here's Mayor Zohran Mamdani earlier this year
making the point, too:

It's not every day that Mayors, even of major cities, are out front on merger
issues, so Mayor Mamdani's statement isn't just compelling as it relates to
this particular merger, but because it's evidence that more and more cities
are starting to think of themselves as agents in the organization of fair and
competitive markets.

Now, cross-border money transfers are also used for less savory purposes.
Since 2001, the U.S. Attorney of Pennsylvania had convicted dozens of Western
Union agents for conspiring with international fraudsters to conduct mass
marketing scams. And there's a relevant connection to Secretary Chopra here,
too. In late 2017, just a few months before Secretary Chopra was himself
appointed to the Federal Trade Commission, Western Union was investigated by
the FTC and agreed to disgorge $586 million after
[admitting](https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-
releases/2017/01/western-union-admits-anti-money-laundering-violations-
settles-consumer-fraud-charges-forfeits-586) to crimes like failing to stem
money laundering schemes and aiding and abetting wire fraud. Fast forward a
few years, while Chopra was serving as Director of the CFPB, that agency
[warned](https://www.paymentsdive.com/news/consumer-financial-protection-
bureau-cfpb-warns-money-transfer-remittance-deceptive-ads-marketing/711751/)
Western Union and other remittance services they should not charge potentially
illegal junk fees. This was not Chopra's first encounter with Western Union
_or_ Intermex.

Since 2025, the Trump Administration has slowed or eviscerated this oversight
work. In August 2025, right as Western Union was announcing its intent to
acquire Intermex, Trump's CFPB was
[cutting](https://www.paymentsdive.com/news/consumer-financial-protection-
bureau-international-money-transfer-oversight/758142/) its oversight of
international money transfer services. When the Western Union
[acquisition](https://ir.westernunion.com/news/archived-press-releases/press-
release-details/2025/Western-Union-and-Intermex-Announce-Expiration-of-the-
Hart-Scott-Rodino-Act-Waiting-Period/default.aspx) of Intermex came before
Trump's FTC in late 2025, the merger didn't get so much as a second look.

That could have been the end of the story. But it wasn't.

### Enter the States

Here's where things get interesting, because federal agencies weren't the only
ones with authority to review the transaction. State level financial
regulators, like those in New York and California, also had authority to
review the acquisition under their respective change of ownership regulations.
And following the election of Mamdani in New York City, the deal started
encountering turbulence, as the mayor [called
on](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/05/13/business/zohran-mamdani-western-union-
intermex.html) the State's Department of Financial Services to review the
merger.

New York financial regulators, in collaboration with NY Attorney General
Letitia James, ultimately [approved](https://ag.ny.gov/press-
release/2026/attorney-general-james-and-new-york-state-department-financial-
services-secure) the merger on August 13, 2026, subject to various commitments
made by Western Union. Those conditions included maintaining all of the
combined company's retail locations throughout the state, continuing to offer
remittance services to key Latin American countries, and capping fee
increases, all for a period of three years following the acquisition.

California financial regulators had also provided tentative approval to the
deal in February 2026, with a built in clock to allow other regulators to
review the deal. But the same day that New York DFS approved the Western
Union-Intermex deal, newly-appointed California Secretary Chopra, who oversees
the State's equivalent financial regulator, suspended its approval of the
merger. The stock prices cratered.

California's authority to review the Western Union-Intermex deal derives from
its licensing regime, which requires anyone who engages in the business of
money transmission to be licensed by the state. Critically, the law also
requires the Department of Financial Protection and Innovation (DFPI) to
approve or disapprove any acquisition of a licensee, which includes the power
to impose conditions in furtherance of the "safety or soundness" of the
licensee, or to enhance consumer protection. That change-of-control authority
is a direct descendant of Governor Johnson's 1911 expansion of the Railroad
Commission.

Fast forward to Tuesday of this week, and California's DFPI announced that it
would _allow_ Western Union to acquire Intermex, but, as in New York, subject
to some [conditions](https://dfpi.ca.gov/press_release/california-imposes-
conditions-on-western-unions-proposed-acquisition-of-major-remittance-
provider-intermex/). Like New York, California prohibited Western Union and
Intermex from shutting down agent locations. Then, California went further in
a couple of ways. First, Western Union would be required to adopt anti-fraud
and anti-money laundering measures. That's basic consumer protection, anti-
crime stuff, if not also a call-back to Chopra's encounters with Western Union
and other remittance services during his time at the FTC and CFPB.

California financial regulators also required Western Union and Intermex to
continue operating , at least partially with respect to a consumer's ability
to choose between their preferred agents, as separate entities. This condition
reflects the state's authority to preserve competition, too, and to make sure
that consumer choice is not sacrificed, even if Western Union and Intermex are
integrating other back-end functions.

Imposing conditions on a licensee has the valence of regulation. And the
authority to impose conditions is expansive. Operating within the bounds of
its statutory authority, the conditions imposed by DFPI did not resemble a
negotiation with private interests, like a mutually-agreed upon consent
decree, but were principally about protecting consumers, preserving market
competition, and enhancing the public interest by whatever means necessary.

However one thinks of it, for Western Union, the prospect of not doing crime
was apparently a raw deal, and Western Union [pulled
out](https://ir.westernunion.com/news/archived-press-releases/press-release-
details/2026/Western-Union-Announces-Termination-of-Agreement-to-Acquire-
Intermex/default.aspx) of its deal to acquire Intermex the next day. Western
Union was not specific as to why, but deemed the conditions "unacceptable,"
adding that they "would have required material changes to Western Union's
business model."

Part of me is skeptical that Western Union was actually frustrated by the
conditions, because I don't see the conditions as anything more than rational
mitigation of the public risk flowing from the combination. While Intermex
shareholders were no doubt looking forward to the payout of a deal, Intermex
seems to be similarly flummoxed by the termination and is
[demanding](https://investors.intermexonline.com/news-releases/news-release-
details/intermex-rejects-western-unions-purported-termination-merger) Western
Union take all steps necessary to consummate the deal subject to DFPI's terms.

So there may still be a thorny road ahead for Western Union and Intermex. In
the meantime, here's former FTC Chair Lina Khan
[celebrating](https://x.com/linamkhan/status/2120578548260028460?s=20) the
outcome:

### People-First Deal-Blocking at the State Level

Khan's final statement is one to sit with: "As newly elected state officials
take the helm in coming months, they will have significant opportunity to use
and activate all their tools to halt corporate abuse and make life better for
working people." While a lot of people are focused on the change of control in
Congress, on a Federal level there is still split government. It is at the
state and local levels where more nimble governance can actually occur.

You can hear in Khan's comments, urging state legislators to "use and activate
all their tools," the echoes of Governor Johnson's clarion call from 1911. And
many state agencies are now possessed of the authority to oversee mergers and
other changes in control that Johnson first established in the state's
Railroad Commission. These kinds of authorities exist across states and cities
that are now controlled by populist Democrats. In 2026, a dozen state
legislative chambers [flipped](https://www.ncsl.org/state-legislatures-
news/details/democratic-wave-upends-republican-dominance-of-state-
legislatures) from red to blue, and a host of administrative positions, from
the Ohio Attorney General to the Texas Agricultural Commission to the Georgia
Public Service Commission, are now run by populists, many of them operating
outside the polarization of left-right politics. I could easily imagine state
and city regulators all over the country reaching out to [block or
regulate](https://www.thebignewsletter.com/p/a-world-without-employees-why-
doordash) mergers like the DoorDash-Instacart transaction.

I know California best, so that's what I'll speak to. In this state, the
California Public Utilities Commission can block a person or corporation from
directly or indirectly merging with, acquiring, or controlling a California
public utility without prior authorization of the Commission. That authority
extends to entities organized outside the State of California, and requires
the Commission to consider things like ratepayer interests, service quality,
and impacts on workers and local economies. There's a specific provision
stating that ratepayers must receive at least 50% of forecasted benefits of
any transaction.

The State's Department of Managed Healthcare and Department of Public Health
are similarly authorized to review and block material changes involving health
insurance plans and the sale of hospitals, skilled nursing facilities, and
other licensed facilities. Similar merger controls exist under the Department
of Cannabis and the Department of Alcohol and Beverage Control, and they also
fall under Secretary Chopra's purview. Veterinary practices, private
cemeteries, pharmacies, and automotive repair businesses do, too.

The California Insurance Commissioner oversees changes in control of insurance
providers. In California, the Insurance Commissioner is an elected statewide
seat, and voters just elected another populist, Jane Kim, to the role.

[![Jane Kim, wearing a gray suit and light pink shirt, smiles with her arms
outstretched toward a person in a white sweater during an outdoor gathering.
Supporters behind her clap and cheer while holding bright pink “Jane Kim”
campaign
signs.](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!rjvS!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F40f0f94f-3c2d-49e4-9f15-2597ec7c2fb1_1023x682.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!rjvS!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F40f0f94f-3c2d-49e4-9f15-2597ec7c2fb1_1023x682.jpeg)

State legislatures are also expanding this authority, interestingly not under
the guise of expanding antitrust law, even though this type of oversight can
serve the same pro-competition and consumer protection ends. California
recently passed a law requiring licensure of small business lenders, an
attempt to give DFPI more authority to oversee usurious merchant cash advance
providers. If you want to be genuinely outraged at the perversity of merchant
cash advances, take a look at this recent
[report](https://protectborrowers.org/what-in-the-giggle-are-we-doing/) by
Protect Borrowers.

The bottom line is that economic fairness, consumer protection, and the
general welfare of workers, consumers and small businesses in the face of
increased corporate concentration is not just a litigation or enforcement
project. It is woven by law into the oversight obligations of little-
recognized bureaucrats. Some of them are captured by the industries they are
commissioned to oversee. Others are more likely to heed the call to advance
the public interest through whatever means necessary, untethered from the
influence of private interests. They will face blowback for doing so, from
business and from the press, but as Governor Johnson recognized, that's the
obvious price for the pursuit of government by and for the people.

As for Governor Johnson, that was a successful political calculation. The rift
within the Republican Party between Taft and the insurgent progressives cost
them the Presidency in 1912. But Johnson would become the first Governor in
California history to serve two consecutive terms in office. He would go on to
serve four terms in the United States Senate. At an inflection point in
California's history, he governed hard and fast, leaving a legacy that just
this week scored another win for Californians and Americans more broadly.
